questions.stem: What distinguishes an infectious disease from other diseases?
options: It is caused by ageing and affects only older members of a population
It is caused by a pathogen and can pass from one host to another
It is caused by a faulty allele inherited from one or both parents
It is caused by poor diet and can be cured by eating a balanced diet
questions.explanation: Infectious diseases result from invasion by a pathogen, such as a bacterium or virus, and can be transmitted. Inherited and dietary diseases are non-infectious and are not passed between hosts.

questions.stem: What is a zoonosis?
options: A disease that is only ever transmitted directly from one human to another human
A disease of plants that is spread from one crop to another by insects feeding
A disease caused by a faulty gene that is shared by many different animal species
A disease that can pass between vertebrate species, such as from birds to humans
questions.explanation: Zoonoses pass between vertebrate species; influenza strains from birds and pigs that infect humans are an example. A disease spread only between humans is not a zoonosis.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes viruses from the other three major groups of pathogens?
options: They are single eukaryotic cells that can move by flagella
They are not cells and can reproduce only inside a host cell
They are prokaryotic cells with a cell wall but with no nucleus
They are eukaryotic cells with walls made of chitin
questions.explanation: Viruses are non-cellular particles of nucleic acid inside a protein coat, and they replicate only by taking over a host cell. The other descriptions fit bacteria, fungi and protists.

questions.stem: A pathogen is a eukaryote with cell walls made of chitin, and it grows as thread-like hyphae that release spores. Which group does it belong to?
options: Protists
Viruses
Fungi
Bacteria
questions.explanation: Chitin cell walls, hyphae and spores are characteristic of fungi. Bacteria are prokaryotes, and protists are mostly single-celled eukaryotes without chitin walls.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes bacteria as pathogens?
options: Eukaryotic, mostly single cells that often have complex life cycles
Prokaryotic cells with a cell wall, no nucleus and a circular chromosome
Eukaryotic cells with a nucleus, mitochondria and chitin-based cell walls
Non-cellular particles made of nucleic acid inside a protein coat
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes: they lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles and have a cell wall. Eukaryotic cells with chitin walls are fungi.

questions.stem: Which pairing of disease and pathogen group is correct?
options: Tuberculosis: bacterium
Malaria: virus
Influenza: fungus
Chytridiomycosis: protist
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Malaria is caused by a protist, influenza by a virus and chytridiomycosis by a fungus.

questions.stem: How is tuberculosis usually transmitted between people?
options: In droplets released into the air when an infected person coughs
In the bite of an infected female mosquito feeding on human blood
In soil carried on boots and vehicles into healthy areas
In contaminated honey stored by infected bee colonies
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis mainly infects the lungs and spreads in airborne droplets, which is why crowded living conditions favour it. Mosquito bites spread malaria and Ross River virus, not tuberculosis.

questions.stem: Crown gall is caused by the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens. How does it produce the tumour-like galls on plants?
options: It enters through the stomata and blocks the xylem, so water builds up into large swellings
It is injected by insects and digests the plant's cell walls to form hollow galls
It infects the leaves and produces spores that grow into galls on the stem
It enters through wounds and transfers DNA that makes plant cells divide uncontrollably
questions.explanation: Agrobacterium enters through wounds near the base of the stem and transfers part of its DNA into plant cells, which then grow and divide abnormally to form a gall. This natural gene transfer is why it is also used in genetic engineering.

questions.stem: How does the amphibian chytrid fungus kill frogs?
options: It infects the liver, so toxic wastes build up in the blood
It infects the skin, disrupting the exchange of water and salts
It infects the lungs, filling them with fluid so that gas exchange stops
It infects red blood cells, which burst and release new spores
questions.explanation: Chytrid infects the keratin of amphibian skin, which frogs use to absorb water and salts, so electrolyte balance fails and the heart stops. It has caused declines and extinctions of frog species worldwide, including in Australia.

questions.stem: Chytrid fungus spreads through streams and ponds. Which feature of its life cycle allows this?
options: It forms airborne spores that are blown long distances between ponds
It is carried in the saliva of mosquitoes that feed on frogs
It survives only inside frogs, so it spreads by direct contact alone
It releases swimming zoospores that move through water to new hosts
questions.explanation: Chytrid produces flagellated zoospores that swim through water and settle on the skin of new hosts. This means it spreads readily wherever amphibians share water, and it can also be carried in wet mud or on equipment.

questions.stem: Which organism transmits the malaria parasite to humans?
options: Male Anopheles mosquitoes
Ticks on kangaroos
Varroa mites
Female Anopheles mosquitoes
questions.explanation: Only female mosquitoes feed on blood, and malaria is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Varroa mites spread viruses among honeybees.

questions.stem: In the malaria life cycle, Plasmodium infects the liver and then red blood cells. Why do patients have repeated bouts of fever?
options: The parasite leaves the body and is re-injected by a new mosquito each time
Liver cells divide rapidly, raising the body temperature each time they split
The patient's own antibiotics destroy the parasites, causing cycles of fever
Infected red blood cells burst together, releasing new parasites and toxins
questions.explanation: Plasmodium multiplies inside red blood cells, which rupture at roughly regular intervals to release new parasites that infect more cells, and each rupture triggers fever. The cycle continues inside the same host without re-infection.

questions.stem: Phytophthora dieback is caused by Phytophthora cinnamomi. How does it kill jarrah and banksia plants?
options: It infects the flowers, so the plant cannot produce any seeds
It rots the roots, so the plant cannot take up enough water
It eats the leaves, so the plant cannot carry out photosynthesis
It blocks the stomata, so the plant cannot carry out gas exchange
questions.explanation: The pathogen attacks the roots and root collar, destroying the tissue that absorbs water, so infected plants die as if from drought. Banksias and many other south-west species are highly susceptible.

questions.stem: Phytophthora cinnamomi was once grouped with the fungi. In which group is it now placed?
options: Protists
Bacteria
Viruses
Plants
questions.explanation: Phytophthora belongs to the oomycetes (water moulds), which have been removed from the Fungi and placed with the protists. Unlike fungi, their cell walls are not made of chitin.

questions.stem: In a jarrah forest, dieback spreads along tracks from an infested area. What is the most likely way it is spreading?
options: Spores blown long distances by strong winds above the trees
Bites of mosquitoes that feed on animals using the tracks
Airborne droplets breathed out by infected native animals
Infested soil carried on vehicles, machinery and footwear
questions.explanation: Phytophthora lives in soil and moves in water and in soil carried on vehicles, boots and machinery, so it spreads along roads and tracks. This is why washdown stations and restricted access are used in dieback areas.

questions.stem: Why are new influenza vaccines needed regularly?
options: The virus mutates rapidly, so its surface proteins keep changing
The vaccine contains antibiotics, which bacteria become resistant to
The virus becomes resistant to each vaccine by forming spores
The vaccine changes the person's genes, which return to normal
questions.explanation: Influenza is an RNA virus that mutates quickly, so its surface proteins change and immunity to last season's strains may not protect against new ones. Vaccines are updated to match the strains expected to circulate.

questions.stem: A new influenza strain arises when a pig is infected with a bird strain and a human strain at once, and the viruses exchange genetic material. Why does such a strain pose a pandemic risk?
options: Few people have immunity to its new combination of surface proteins
It is a bacterium and so cannot be treated with any of the antibiotics
It can spread only between pigs, so humans cannot be infected
It has lost all of its genes, so it replicates much faster
questions.explanation: Mixing genes from different strains can produce a virus with surface proteins the human population has not met, so almost no one is immune and it can spread worldwide. This is why influenza is a zoonosis that health agencies monitor closely.

questions.stem: Ross River virus is the most common mosquito-borne disease of humans in Australia. Which animals are its main natural reservoir hosts?
options: Domestic cats and dogs
Freshwater fish and frogs
Honeybees and native bees
Kangaroos and wallabies
questions.explanation: Mosquitoes pick up Ross River virus from infected macropods, such as kangaroos and wallabies, and pass it to humans. Humans develop joint pain, rashes and fatigue.

questions.stem: Ross River virus cases in south-west WA often rise after high tides and heavy rain in warm months. What is the best explanation?
options: High tides carry infected fish into estuaries where people often swim
Cooler, wetter weather makes kangaroos move into towns and bite people
Water pooling in salt marshes and wetlands creates more mosquito breeding sites
Rain washes the virus out of the soil, so more people then inhale it from the air
questions.explanation: Mosquito larvae develop in still water, so tidal flooding and rain increase breeding, and warm temperatures speed up the mosquito life cycle. More mosquitoes feeding on reservoir hosts and people means more transmission.

questions.stem: How does the Varroa mite contribute to viral disease in honeybees?
options: It is a virus itself, one that infects the wings of developing bees
It produces a toxin that makes bees resistant to most viruses
It kills the queen so the colony cannot raise any new workers
It feeds on bees and transmits viruses such as deformed wing virus
questions.explanation: Varroa is a parasitic mite that feeds on developing and adult bees and acts as a vector, spreading viruses such as deformed wing virus through the colony. Infected bees may emerge with crumpled, useless wings.

questions.stem: Why does the life cycle of a pathogen, including how it invades and leaves its host, affect its success?
options: It must kill its host quickly so that it can feed on the body
It must remain inside one host for life to avoid all predators
It must avoid reproducing until the host has become very old
It must reach new hosts before the current host dies or recovers
questions.explanation: A pathogen survives only if it is transmitted, so its mode of transmission and its impact on the host must allow it to reach new hosts. A pathogen that kills its host before spreading dies out with it.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors would most favour the rapid spread of a disease through a population?
options: Fast pathogen growth, a dense host population and airborne transmission
Slow pathogen growth, a sparse host population and airborne transmission
Fast pathogen growth, a sparse host population and transmission by blood
Slow pathogen growth, a dense host population and transmission by blood
questions.explanation: Spread depends on how quickly the pathogen multiplies, how close together hosts are and how easily it passes between them. Rapid multiplication, crowding and airborne spread together allow many new infections quickly.

questions.stem: Why is a disease transmitted by direct contact likely to spread faster in a crowded city than in a remote farming area?
options: A lower host density means that each infected person meets more uninfected people
Pathogens grow faster in cities because the air there is warmer and drier
People in cities have more antibodies, so the pathogen evolves to spread faster
A higher host density means more contacts between infected and uninfected people
questions.explanation: When hosts are packed closely together, each infected person contacts more susceptible people, so transmission increases. High population density in urban areas is one reason for susceptibility to epidemics.

questions.stem: Why has increasing global travel made epidemics and pandemics more likely?
options: Aircraft cabins produce new pathogens from the air they recycle
Travellers become immune and spread their immunity to others
Long flights cause mutations that make all pathogens less harmful
Infected people can carry a pathogen to distant regions within a day
questions.explanation: Air travel can move an infected person across the world before symptoms appear, so outbreaks spread between countries quickly. Regional and global movement of organisms facilitates transmission.

questions.stem: Climate models predict warmer, wetter conditions in some regions further from the equator. What is a likely effect on mosquito-borne diseases?
options: Their range will shrink to the equator, because rain kills the mosquito larvae
Their range may spread to new areas where the mosquito vectors can now survive
They will disappear, because mosquitoes cannot breed when conditions get warmer
They will no longer need a vector and will spread from person to person instead
questions.explanation: Mosquito survival and breeding depend on temperature and standing water, so warmer, wetter conditions can let vectors, and the diseases they carry, establish in new regions. Mosquito larvae need water, so rain helps rather than kills them.

questions.stem: Why do many pathogens evolve rapidly in a changing environment?
options: They choose to mutate whenever a host's environment becomes hostile to them
They reproduce sexually only when antibiotics are present in the host
They have very long generation times, so each mutation has time to spread
They breed fast in huge numbers, so mutations arise and spread quickly
questions.explanation: Bacteria and viruses can produce many generations in a day, so new mutations appear often and natural selection spreads any advantageous ones quickly. Mutations arise randomly; pathogens do not choose to mutate.

questions.stem: A doctor declines to prescribe antibiotics for a patient with influenza. Why?
options: Influenza is a virus, and antibiotics target structures found only in bacteria
Influenza is a bacterium that has a thick, waterproof outer wall made of chitin
Influenza is a protist that hides inside red blood cells, out of reach
Influenza is a fungus that breaks antibiotics down using its own enzymes
questions.explanation: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures such as cell walls and bacterial ribosomes, which viruses lack. Viral infections are treated with antiviral drugs that interfere with viral replication.

questions.stem: How do antiviral drugs disrupt the life cycle of a virus?
options: They break down the cell walls of the virus so that it bursts open
They kill the bacteria that carry viruses from one host to another
They make host cells divide faster so that the virus is diluted
They interfere with stages of viral replication or release from host cells
questions.explanation: Antivirals target steps such as viral entry, copying of the viral genome or release of new particles from infected cells. Viruses have no cell walls, so drugs that attack walls work only on bacteria.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes herd immunity?
options: Immunity gained only after every member of the population has been infected
Protection gained by keeping animals away from all human populations
Protection of non-immune people because enough of the population is immune
Immunity that a whole herd of animals inherits from a single resistant parent
questions.explanation: When a high enough proportion of people are immune, chains of transmission break, so those who cannot be vaccinated are less likely to meet the pathogen. It does not require everyone to be infected or immune.

questions.stem: The proportion of a population that must be immune for herd immunity is about 1 − 1/R, where R is the average number of people one case infects in a non-immune population. If R = 4, what proportion must be immune?
questions.explanation: 1 − 1/4 = 0.75, so about 75% of people must be immune. A more transmissible pathogen with a larger R needs an even higher level of immunity.

questions.stem: Which is an example of disrupting a pathogen's life cycle to control a vector-borne disease?
options: Treating a patient's fever with a cooling medicine
Isolating patients whose disease is spread by mosquitoes alone
Draining standing water where mosquito larvae develop
Prescribing antibiotics to a person with influenza
questions.explanation: Removing breeding sites reduces the number of mosquitoes, breaking the cycle between hosts. Influenza is a virus, so antibiotics do not affect it, and treating a fever eases symptoms without touching the pathogen.

questions.stem: Which is a physical preventative measure against a mosquito-borne disease?
options: Taking antimalarial drugs before travel
Sleeping under an insecticide-treated bed net
Taking a course of antiviral tablets
Being vaccinated against the pathogen
questions.explanation: A bed net is a physical barrier that stops mosquitoes biting at night. Vaccines and drugs act on the immune system or the pathogen rather than physically blocking contact.

questions.stem: Vehicles entering a dieback-free area of jarrah forest must pass through a washdown station. Which management strategy is this?
options: Herd immunity created by planting resistant trees nearby
Quarantine and hygiene to stop infested soil entering the area
Immunisation of the trees so that they resist infection
Antibiotic treatment of soil to kill bacteria in the roots
questions.explanation: Washing soil off vehicles and limiting access stop Phytophthora being carried into healthy areas, a form of quarantine. Phytophthora is not a bacterium, and plants cannot be immunised like animals.

questions.stem: Why does Australia inspect incoming cargo, mail and travellers' luggage at its borders?
options: To measure how many pathogens Australians already carry
To stop exotic pests and diseases harming agriculture and the environment
To stop native species and their diseases from leaving the country
To make sure all imported plants are genetically modified
questions.explanation: Quarantine measures protect Australia's agriculture and natural environment from disease-carrying materials and organisms, which matters more as trade and travel increase. Australia is free of many pests and diseases found elsewhere.

questions.stem: What is a major use of computer models of disease spread?
options: To replace the need to collect any data from real outbreaks
To predict an outbreak's course and test interventions such as vaccination
To produce vaccines directly from the data entered into the model
To prove exactly how many people will be infected in a given year
questions.explanation: Models use data on population size and density, transmission and other variables to predict spread and simulate the effects of possible interventions. Their predictions depend on the quality of the data and assumptions, so they are not certain.

questions.stem: Why is international cooperation important when a new viral disease emerges?
options: Cooperation stops viruses from mutating as they cross borders
Shared data and early warnings let countries assess and contain the risk
Each country can then close its borders without telling the others
Viruses can be studied in only one laboratory in the world
questions.explanation: Diseases do not stop at borders, so sharing information about cases, genomes and spread lets countries evaluate the risk and act early. Cooperation does not affect how a virus mutates.

questions.stem: Two countries have the same outbreak. Country X has many clinics, testing and vaccines; Country Y has few. Why is Country Y more susceptible to an epidemic?
options: Cases are found and treated later, so more transmission occurs before control
Pathogens mutate faster in countries that have fewer clinics and doctors
People in Country Y are born with fewer alleles for resisting disease
Vaccines in Country X spread through the air and protect its neighbours
questions.explanation: Varied healthcare systems affect how quickly cases are detected, isolated and treated and how many people are vaccinated, so weaker systems allow more spread. Mutation rate does not depend on the number of clinics.
